cf.title: Proposal: Include CHECK constraint expression in violation error DETAIL

input.subject: Proposal: Include CHECK constraint expression in violation error DETAIL

verdict_reasoning: The goal is plausible and the change is small, but the thread has not yet agreed that it is wanted. demand-1 and already-exists-1 survive: the only stated case is a saved lookup step, and the error already carries the constraint name as an error field. The verdict rests on absence of evidence in a three-week-old thread with one reviewer, so confidence is low. The level 2 objections that survived are fixable but were not evaluated.

brief.title: Include CHECK constraint expression in violation error DETAIL
brief.problem: When a CHECK constraint fails, the error names the constraint and shows the failing row but not the condition. Users must run \d or read the catalog to see what was violated.
brief.proposed_design: ExecRelCheck returns the failed ConstrCheck instead of only its name. ExecConstraints then deparses ccbin and appends the expression to the existing DETAIL line. When the failing-row detail is suppressed for lack of privileges, the whole DETAIL, expression included, is omitted.
user_visible_surface: Changed DETAIL text for CHECK violations: "Failing row contains (...). Check constraint expression: (age >= 18)."
Same changed DETAIL text in the server log.
author_claims: Showing the expression saves users a step of inspecting the table definition.
The expression is not shown when the failing row is hidden, so no new information reaches clients or the log in that case.
A reviewer argued any role can already read CHECK expressions from the catalog, so no permission check is needed; the author agreed.
v2 updates regression expected output and all regression tests pass.
brief.thread_state: One reviewer, Yash Jadhav, discussed security and found no extra control needed; the author agreed and posted v2 with updated test output. No committer has replied, and nobody has discussed whether the change is wanted.
unclear: The patch has no documentation change, and the thread does not say whether the DETAIL format is documented anywhere.
The thread does not discuss long or complex expressions, which could make DETAIL very long.
The thread does not say whether domain CHECK violations and other constraint errors change too; domain.out is touched but not explained.
The thread does not discuss tools or tests outside core that parse the DETAIL text.
The thread does not say whether the expression uses the same deparse output as pg_get_constraintdef, including schema qualification.
The thread does not measure the cost of deparsing the expression at error time.

prior_attempts.title: Mention column name in error messages
prior_attempts.quote: If it isn't, we'd be best off to reject this patch rather than create an expectation among users that such context should be there.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane found that the callback only covers errors raised during parse analysis or constant folding, not run-time errors from non-constant expressions, and covering those would need executor changes with a likely performance cost. He argued that partial coverage would mislead users and that the cases it handles already have error cursor information. He proposed extending error cursor support into execution instead, and Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P7 added column context to type coercion errors through a parse-analysis callback, so it missed run-time errors. This patch changes the executor path that raises table CHECK violations, so it has no comparable gap within that error class.

objections.title: No demand shown beyond the author's own wish
objections.failure_scenario: A committer weighs a change to every CHECK violation message against one person's request. Nothing in the thread shows users struggling today, so the change risks churn for a problem nobody reported.
objections.argument: The only motivation is message #1: users "need to inspect the table with \d". No -general or -bugs reports, no other users and no comparison with other database systems appear. Message #2 reviews security, not need, and nobody in the thread discusses whether the change is wanted. The error already names the constraint and sets the constraint-name error field, so a client can call pg_get_constraintdef, and descriptive constraint names cover most cases.
objections.author_must_show: Which users or reports show that the constraint name plus \d or pg_get_constraintdef is not enough in practice?

critic.reasoning: The thread has one reviewer, who discussed security only, and no reports or other users asking for this. The thread is three weeks old, so this is a request to show demand and not a ground for rejection.

objections.title: Constraint name and error fields already lead to the expression
objections.failure_scenario: Every CHECK violation, in every application and every server log, carries a longer DETAIL line. Users who already look up the constraint by name gain nothing from it. Logs fill with copies of expressions that are already stored in pg_constraint.
objections.argument: The error already names the constraint and carries the schema, table and constraint names as separate error fields. A client or user can read the condition from \d or from pg_get_constraintdef() on the matching pg_constraint row, and message #2 notes that any role can read these. The proposal therefore makes the lookup more convenient but does not make anything possible that was not possible before. The author's case is "saves users a step" (message #1), and the thread has no field reports or user requests showing that this step is a real burden.
objections.author_must_show: Which users cannot practically look up the expression from the constraint name or the error fields today, and how often does this happen?

critic.reasoning: CHECK violations already carry schema, table and constraint names as error fields, and any role can read the expression from the catalog. The author's only stated case is a saved step, which does not by itself answer the desirability question.

other_surviving.title: Only table CHECK errors gain the expression; similar constraint errors do not
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A user learns that CHECK violations show the violated condition. Later the same user hits a partition constraint or domain CHECK violation, sees only the name, and has to go back to \d. Support tooling written around the new DETAIL text works for one error family and not the next.
other_surviving.argument: The commit message changes only ExecConstraints for table CHECK constraints. The thread does not say whether partition constraint, domain CHECK or NOT NULL errors change, and domain.out is touched without explanation. In [P7] the recorded reason against partial context was that it creates "an expectation among users that such context should be there" when coverage is incomplete. Error wording for related constraint kinds is usually kept parallel.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which constraint violation errors change, which do not, and why is that line the right place to stop?

precedents.title: Mention column name in error messages

critic.reasoning: The thread and commit message do not say which constraint errors change, and domain.out is touched without explanation. [P7] concerned partial coverage inside one error class, so it is weak support; the consistency question stands without it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Every CHECK violation logs the full deparsed expression, with no opt-out
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A site has a CHECK with a long IN list and a batch job that rejects many rows. After upgrade, each logged error carries the whole expression, so log volume grows sharply and the readable part of the message is pushed out of view. The operator finds out when log disks fill or log shipping falls behind.
other_surviving.argument: The proposal adds the expression to DETAIL for every violation, and message #3 confirms the server log gets the same text. The thread says nothing about long expressions, truncation or a size cap. This is a behaviour change for existing installations that did not ask for it, while the information can already be read from the catalog.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does the DETAIL behave for a CHECK expression of several kilobytes, and why is no truncation or opt-out needed?

critic.reasoning: The existing failing-row text truncates each column value, but the proposal sets no bound on the expression. The thread does not discuss long expressions, and message #3 confirms the same text goes to the server log.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Ties ruleutils deparse output to every CHECK violation message
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how ruleutils prints casts, parentheses or schema qualification. Expected output for CHECK violations then changes in core regression files and in the test suites of extensions and applications. Those suites fail on the next major release, and their maintainers update them by hand.
other_surviving.argument: v2 already touches eleven expected files for one message, so the coupling is wide on day one. Deparse output depends on search_path and on ruleutils formatting choices, which change across releases, while the current message depends only on the constraint name. The proposal does not say whether the output matches pg_get_constraintdef or how stable it is meant to be.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which deparse rules, including schema qualification and search_path, does the DETAIL follow, and why is linking it to ruleutils changes acceptable for downstream test suites?

critic.reasoning: Deparse output varies with search_path, so the same violation can produce different DETAIL text, and the proposal does not say which deparse rules it follows. The churn in expected files is routine, but the open question about output rules is real.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: Every CHECK violation now pays for deparsing, including caught errors
refuted.failure_scenario: An application loads rows in a PL/pgSQL loop and catches check_violation to skip bad rows. Each violation now runs a ruleutils deparse with catalog lookups, even though nobody reads the DETAIL. A table with a CHECK on a long IN list also writes that whole list to the server log for every rejected row.
refuted.argument: The DETAIL is built before ereport, so the deparse runs whether the error is logged, sent to a client, or caught by an exception block. The thread measures neither this error-path cost nor DETAIL length for large expressions. Using exceptions for flow control is common enough that this cost lands on users who never asked for the expression. Log volume grows with expression size, and no setting turns the new text off.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a loop that catches many check_violation errors cost before and after the patch, and how is DETAIL bounded for very long expressions?

critic.reasoning: The existing code already builds the failing-row text before ereport, and a caught error already pays for a subtransaction abort. Nothing shows that one deparse adds a material cost to that; the log volume part is a duplicate of standards-compat-2.

refuted.title: Constraint name is already a structured field clients can resolve
refuted.failure_scenario: A user hits a CHECK error and wants the condition. The error already carries the schema, table and constraint names as separate fields, so psql or a driver could call pg_get_constraintdef on demand. Instead every server pays for the lookup on every violation, and NOT NULL, foreign key and exclusion errors stay unchanged.
refuted.argument: The only benefit claimed is saving one lookup step, and the thread shows no field reports or demand beyond message #1. The same argument would justify adding definitions to foreign key, exclusion and domain errors, which is the accumulation item 5 warns about. Nobody in the thread has discussed whether the change is wanted, or whether a client-side lookup would be enough.
refuted.author_must_show: Why must the server deparse the expression when clients already receive the constraint name as a field, and should other constraint errors follow?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1, which states the existing-alternative point without the unmeasured server cost claim.

refuted.title: Every user pays for changed DETAIL text, few gain
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension author or application team upgrades and finds that regression expected output and log-parsing rules no longer match every CHECK violation. Tables with long CHECK expressions also write longer DETAIL lines to the server log on every failed insert.
refuted.argument: v2 changes expected output in eleven regression files, which suggests how many out-of-core test suites and log tools would also change. The gain goes only to users who cannot easily look up the constraint. The thread does not discuss this trade-off, or a way to limit the change to users who want it.
refuted.author_must_show: What benefit to users outweighs breaking existing expected output and log parsers that match CHECK violation DETAIL text?

critic.reasoning: Any change to message wording alters expected output and text-matching log rules; Postgres does not keep DETAIL text stable, and clients have SQLSTATE and error fields for matching. The log length part is a duplicate of standards-compat-2.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The CHECK expression goes to clients and the server log, and is dropped only when the failing-row detail is suppressed.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The DETAIL text of every CHECK violation now depends on ruleutils deparse output; v2 changes eleven expected files.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The expression is already reachable from the constraint name through \d or pg_get_constraintdef().

questions: Which users or reports show that the constraint name plus \d or pg_get_constraintdef() is not enough in practice?
Why must the server add the expression when clients already receive the schema, table and constraint names as error fields?
Which constraint violation errors change (table CHECK, domain CHECK, partition constraint), which do not, and why stop there?
How does the DETAIL behave for a CHECK expression of several kilobytes, and is truncation needed as for failing-row values?
Does the DETAIL follow the same deparse rules as pg_get_constraintdef(), including schema qualification under different search_path settings?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows executor constraint checking and error reporting, and the ruleutils deparse code.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the wording and length of every CHECK violation DETAIL, in clients and in the server log, and for its dependence on ruleutils output in later releases.
committability.author_follow_up: The author wrote in message #1 that he wants to continue developing the patch, and posted v2 with updated test output within a week of the review.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: Reports from -general or -bugs, support cases, or several independent users on the thread who say the lookup step is a real burden, for example where the person reading the error or log cannot query the catalog. A committer saying the change is wanted would also settle it.

priority.reason: The patch changes one executor file plus expected output, and adds no new setting or format. The thread has one reviewer, who discussed security only, so it needs a committer or more users to say whether the change is wanted.

provisional_note: The code was not read. It could not be checked whether domain CHECK or partition constraint errors change, which deparse context and search_path rules the expression uses, or whether the expression length is bounded.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: clean up create|alter domain stmt incompatiable constraint error case and add regression test
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch added broader regression tests for CREATE DOMAIN and ALTER DOMAIN (DefineDomain had low test coverage) and cleaned up error handling for incompatible domain constraints. It replaced the unhelpful "unrecognized constraint subtype" error for generated-column constraints on domains with a clear message, and made ALTER DOMAIN ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... NO INHERIT NOT VALID fail.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was withdrawn because the patch had been folded into a later patch version (v6) in another thread. A reviewer asked whether this separate commitfest entry should therefore be closed. No objection to the content of the patch is shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Looks like this patch is now part of v6 from here [0]. Should we close
[1] CF entry?

precedents_retrieved.title: NLS: use gettext() to translate system error messages
precedents_retrieved.summary: Translate the system error text substituted for %m with gettext and Postgres's own .po files, instead of relying on strerror_r() translation. This makes errno messages follow NLS on every platform and stops depending on LC_CTYPE.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that platforms whose strerror() does not translate leave their users used to untranslated errno strings, so Postgres should behave like other programs on the platform. He also objected to putting the translation in snprintf.c and noted that the implementation was not thread-safe. The author marked the entry rejected because there was no consensus to proceed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If it doesn't, then the users of that platform are unaccustomed to
seeing translated errno strings, and they are unlikely to thank us
for behaving differently from every other program on the platform.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve amcheck to check UNIQUE constraint in btree index
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Peter Geoghegan, Mark Dilger, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend contrib/amcheck's bt_index_check and bt_index_parent_check so that, for btree indexes with a UNIQUE constraint, they detect duplicate keys whose heap tuples are visible, including duplicates spanning adjacent leaf pages, and report the index and heap TIDs involved. Later versions added an optional argument to enable the uniqueness check and a regression test variant for 32-bit systems.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers asked for further changes: Peter Geoghegan objected to reporting violations as WARNINGs, to the message saying an index only might be corrupt (calling it an unacceptable false positive), to the handling of cross-page duplicates, and to tests that update pg_index, and suggested opclass-based fault injection and sharing the heapallindexed snapshot. Mark Dilger's review of v4 asked for documentation updates, pg_amcheck integration with TAP tests, and a different test approach. No updated patch followed for several weeks, and David Steele marked it Returned with Feedback because it needed more work and had not been updated.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch appears to need some work and has not been updated in several
weeks, so marking Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Bug: wrong relname in RemoveSubscriptionRel() error detail
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the error detail in RemoveSubscriptionRel() to name the relation from the current pg_subscription_rel row (subrel->srrelid) instead of the relid argument. The author asked for a back-patch, since relid can be InvalidOid while the loop scans mapping rows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers showed that no current caller can hit the error with an invalid relid. The error path needs an invalid subid, and the only such caller, heap_drop_with_catalog(), always passes a valid relid. Amit Kapila saw no concrete case that needs the change. The author agreed that no current use case triggers it and dropped the back-patch request, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I feel unless we have
some concrete case it may not be beneficial to change it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Mention column name in error messages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the target column name to errors raised when a value cannot be coerced to a column's type in INSERT or ALTER COLUMN, for example "value too long for type character varying(4)". After review, the first version, which changed datatype input functions, was reworked to use an error context callback in the parser.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reviewed the patch and asked for code cleanups and tests, since the patch had none. The author did not reply, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback two months after that review because the comments had not been addressed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Patch is marked as returned with feedback, it has been two months
since the last review, and comments have not been addressed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Mention column name in error messages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the target column name and type to errors raised when a value is coerced into an insert or update column, such as "value too long for type character varying(4)". After review it used an error context callback set up during parse analysis of assigned expressions instead of changing datatype input functions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found that the callback only covers errors raised during parse analysis or constant folding, not run-time errors from non-constant expressions, and covering those would need executor changes with a likely performance cost. He argued that partial coverage would mislead users and that the cases it handles already have error cursor information. He proposed extending error cursor support into execution instead, and Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If it isn't,
we'd be best off to reject this patch rather than create an expectation
among users that such context should be there.

precedents_retrieved.title: CHECK constraint deferrable Support
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets CHECK constraints be declared DEFERRABLE and INITIALLY DEFERRED, as the SQL standard allows, so SET CONSTRAINTS can delay a CHECK until commit. Rows that fail a deferrable CHECK are rechecked at commit time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the CHECK implementation assumes constraints are immutable, and the patch does not change that assumption, so he called the feature a toy. Others then argued it should be dropped or combined with deferrable NOT NULL, which Robert Haas and Vik Fearing disputed. Dean Rasheed also reported open bugs, including a deferred constraint that still failed immediately and a wrong constraint-exclusion result. The visible messages do not show why the author withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I continue to assert that basing this feature on the current CHECK implementation will produce nothing but a toy feature, that's not only of little practical use but will be an active foot-gun for people who expect it to do more than it can.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix pg_get_constraintdef for NOT NULL constraints on domains
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix pg_get_constraintdef for NOT NULL constraints on domains
Reverted commit(s): Revert structural changes to not-null constraints
precedents_retrieved.objection:
We added pg_constraint rows for all not-null constraints, first for
tables and later for domains; but while the ones for tables were
reverted, the ones for domains were not.  However, we did accidentally
revert ruleutils.c support for the ones on domains in 6f8bb7c1e961,
which breaks running pg_get_constraintdef() on them.  Put that back.

This is only needed in branch 17, because we've reinstated this code in
branch master with commit 14e87ffa5c54.  Add some new tests in both
branches.

I couldn't find anything else that needs de-reverting.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow to warn or error on ... = NULL expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend the transform_null_equals setting from a boolean to an enum with off, warn, error and on values, so that "expr = NULL" expressions can produce a warning or the SQL-standard error. The original patch made 'warn' the default; later versions kept the existing behaviour as the default.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected to making 'warn' the default because "foo = NULL" is legal SQL, and saw little value in the warn mode, since such queries can be found with grep. Bruce Momjian considered this one check not useful enough on its own and wanted it to be part of a wider "novice" mode that warns about bad SQL practices. Dmitry Dolgov asked what such a mode should include, received no response, and marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I will again say I would love to see this as part of a wholesale
"novice" mode which warns of generally bad SQL practices.  I don't see
this one item alone as sufficiently useful.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add GUC backtrace_on_internal_error"
Reverted commit(s): Add GUC backtrace_on_internal_error
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit a740b213d4b4d3360ad0cac696e47e5ec0eb8864.

Subsequent discussion showed that there was interest in a more general
facility to configure when server log events would produce backtraces,
and this existing limited way couldn't be extended in a compatible
way.  So the consensus was to revert this for PostgreSQL 17 and
reconsider this topic for PostgreSQL 18.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent records a rejection of showing the constraint expression. P7's partial-coverage reason fits this patch only weakly, because domain CHECK errors and partition constraint errors use other paths, and the thread has not raised that. P6 ended because the author did not reply, which does not apply here.
The change to DETAIL text is not treated as a compatibility break, because message text is not a stable interface and the thread does not show anyone relying on it.

The proposal only changes the text of the DETAIL field for CHECK violations; it adds no on-disk, WAL, catalog, protocol message or replication state. ExecRelCheck is internal to execMain.c, so the changed return type should not affect the extension ABI, though this cannot be confirmed without the code.

The expression text is already readable by any role through pg_constraint and pg_get_constraintdef, and v2 drops it with the whole DETAIL when the failing row is hidden. With column-level privileges, a partial row shows only permitted values, and a referenced hidden column exposes only its name, which the catalog already shows. I found no new leak, escalation path or denial-of-service risk that I could tie to a concrete scenario.

One objection: the need is already met by existing mechanisms, so the proposal adds convenience only. The listed precedents concern column names in coercion errors, and their recorded reasons do not apply here.
Demand is not shown, but the idea is small and plausible. These are 'not now, show demand' objections, not a rejection.
